title: Celiac disease · HLA-DQ2.5 tag (HLA-DQA1)
summary: Nearly all people with celiac disease carry the HLA-DQ2.5 or HLA-DQ8 molecules that present gluten fragments to the immune system. rs2187668 is a well-validated tag for the DQ2.5 haplotype: the T allele marks DQ2.5 carriage. Carrying DQ2.5 is close to necessary but far from sufficient — roughly a quarter of many populations carry it, while about 1% develop celiac disease.

interpretations.CC: No copies of the DQ2.5 tag allele. This makes carriage of the highest-risk celiac haplotype unlikely, which on average substantially lowers the genetic predisposition to celiac disease. It does not rule it out: DQ8 and DQ2.2, tagged by other variants, also confer susceptibility, and tag SNPs are imperfect proxies compared with direct HLA typing.
interpretations.CT: One copy of the T allele tagging HLA-DQ2.5, the haplotype found in roughly 90% of people with celiac disease. Carriers have higher average odds of celiac disease than non-carriers, but the vast majority of DQ2.5 carriers — around 25-30% of many populations — never develop it. This is a susceptibility marker, not a prediction.
interpretations.TT: Two copies of the T allele, consistent with carrying HLA-DQ2.5 on both chromosomes. Studies associate a double dose of DQ2.5 with higher average odds of celiac disease than a single copy. Even so, most people with this genotype never develop celiac disease; genotype describes predisposition only.

title: Type 1 diabetes · HLA DR3-DQ2 / DR4-DQ8 tags
summary: The HLA region is by far the largest genetic contributor to type 1 diabetes, with the DR3-DQ2 and DR4-DQ8 haplotypes carrying most of that signal. Two tag variants approximate them: the rs2187668 T allele tags DR3-DQ2 and the rs7454108 C allele tags DR4-DQ8. Carrying one of each (the DR3/DR4 combination) is associated with the highest average risk, though most carriers of any of these haplotypes never develop type 1 diabetes.

interpretations.CC: No copies of the DR3-DQ2 tag. This lowers the average HLA-based risk from that form. DR4-DQ8, shown below, and other HLA types also matter. Tag variants are imperfect stand-ins for direct HLA typing.
interpretations.CT: One copy of the T allele tagging DR3-DQ2, one of the two major type 1 diabetes susceptibility haplotypes. Its impact depends heavily on what the other haplotype is: the DR3/DR4 combination is associated with the highest average odds. Even in that highest group, the large majority of carriers never develop type 1 diabetes.
interpretations.TT: Two copies of the T allele, consistent with DR3-DQ2 on both chromosomes. DR3 homozygosity is associated with clearly elevated average odds of type 1 diabetes relative to non-carriers, though lower on average than the DR3/DR4 combination. Absolute risk remains modest for most carriers.

No copies of the tag for the DR4-DQ8 haplotype. This lowers the average HLA-based susceptibility contributed by DQ8, one of the two haplotypes carrying most of the HLA signal in type 1 diabetes. Other HLA haplotypes, including DR3-DQ2, still contribute, and a tag SNP is only a proxy for direct HLA typing.
interpretations.CT: One copy of the C allele tagging DR4-DQ8, a major type 1 diabetes susceptibility haplotype. Combined with a DR3-DQ2 copy at the companion variant, this corresponds to the DR3/DR4 genotype associated with the highest average odds. Most carriers of DQ8, including DR3/DR4 carriers, never develop type 1 diabetes.
interpretations.CC: Two copies of the C allele, consistent with DR4-DQ8 on both chromosomes. DQ8 homozygosity is associated with elevated average odds of type 1 diabetes relative to non-carriers. This remains a probabilistic association; the large majority of people with this genotype are unaffected.

title: Rheumatoid arthritis · PTPN22 R620W
summary: PTPN22 encodes a phosphatase that dampens immune-cell signaling. The R620W missense variant (rs2476601) is one of the strongest common non-HLA risk factors for rheumatoid arthritis. Each copy is linked to higher odds of seropositive disease: a moderate shift. It also shows associations with type 1 diabetes and other autoimmune conditions. Note that on GRCh38 the reference allele A corresponds to the risk (620W) form; G is the common non-risk allele.

interpretations.AA: Two copies of risk-linked A (620W), found in about 1% of people with European ancestry. Studies link this result to several times the average odds of antibody-positive rheumatoid arthritis versus GG. It is also linked to some other autoimmune conditions. Most people with this result are never affected.
interpretations.AG: One copy of the risk-associated A allele (620W). Linked on average to higher odds of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis than GG: a moderate shift. This is one susceptibility factor among many genetic and environmental influences, including smoking. It does not predict disease.
interpretations.GG: Two copies of the common G allele (620R). This genotype does not carry the PTPN22 R620W risk association; average odds of rheumatoid arthritis at this variant are the population baseline. Many other genetic and environmental factors still shape overall susceptibility.

citations.label: Begovich et al., Am J Hum Genet 2004

title: Multiple sclerosis · HLA-DRB1*15:01 tag
summary: HLA-DRB1*15:01 is the strongest genetic risk factor for multiple sclerosis. Each copy is linked to higher odds: a moderate to large shift. rs3135388 is a widely used tag for this HLA allele: the A allele marks DRB1*15:01 carriage (on GRCh38 the reference base at this position is the tag allele A). Because MS affects well under 1% of most populations, even the elevated odds in carriers leave absolute risk low.

interpretations.AA: Two copies of A, which tags HLA-DRB1*15:01. Studies link two copies to several times the odds of multiple sclerosis versus no copies. MS is rare, so most people with this result do not develop it. This is one factor among many, including EBV exposure and vitamin D.
interpretations.AG: One copy of the A allele tagging HLA-DRB1*15:01, carried by roughly 15-30% of people of European ancestry. Linked on average to higher odds of multiple sclerosis than non-carriers: a moderate to large shift. Because MS is uncommon, absolute risk remains low; this is a single susceptibility factor, not a prediction.
interpretations.GG: No copies of the DRB1*15:01 tag allele. Average odds of multiple sclerosis at this locus are at or slightly below the population baseline. Other genetic variants and environmental factors still contribute, and a tag SNP is an imperfect proxy for direct HLA typing.

citations.label: Hafler et al. (IMSGC), N Engl J Med 2007

title: Crohn's disease · NOD2 (R702W, G908R)
summary: NOD2 is a sensor inside immune cells that detects pieces of bacterial cell walls. Its variants were the first genetic risk factors found for Crohn’s disease. R702W (rs2066844) and G908R (rs2066845) are each linked to higher odds per copy: a moderate to large shift. Two NOD2 risk copies, including a frameshift not shown here, are linked to much higher odds. The link is strongest when Crohn’s affects the last part of the small intestine.

interpretations.CC: Two copies of the common C allele — no R702W variant. Average odds of Crohn's disease at this variant are the population baseline. NOD2 has other risk variants (G908R below, and a frameshift, 1007fs, that this report does not cover), and most Crohn's risk lies outside NOD2 altogether.
interpretations.CT: One copy of the T allele encoding R702W, the most common NOD2 risk variant in European-ancestry populations (about 4-5% allele frequency). Associated on average with higher odds of Crohn’s disease: a moderate to large shift. Because Crohn’s affects well under 1% of people, most carriers are never affected.
interpretations.TT: Two copies of the T allele encoding R702W. Carrying two NOD2 risk-variant copies is associated in studies with substantially higher average odds of Crohn’s disease — a large shift, often with ileal involvement. Even so, absolute risk remains limited, and many people with two copies stay unaffected.

interpretations.GG: Two copies of the common G allele — no G908R variant. Average odds of Crohn's disease at this variant are the population baseline. Other NOD2 variants (R702W above, and the 1007fs frameshift not covered here) and many non-NOD2 factors still contribute to overall susceptibility.
interpretations.CG: One copy of the C allele encoding G908R, a NOD2 risk variant carried by roughly 1-2% of European-ancestry chromosomes. Associated on average with higher odds of Crohn’s disease: a moderate to large shift. Most carriers never develop Crohn’s disease; this is one susceptibility factor among many.
interpretations.CC: Two copies of the C allele encoding G908R — a rare genotype. Two NOD2 risk-variant copies are associated with substantially higher average odds of Crohn's disease, often with ileal involvement. This remains a probabilistic association rather than a prediction, and many such carriers stay unaffected.

title: Psoriasis · HLA-C*06:02 tag
summary: HLA-C*06:02 is the major genetic risk factor for psoriasis, especially early-onset and guttate forms. Each copy is linked to higher odds in most populations: a moderate to large shift. rs10484554 is a commonly used tag for this HLA allele: the T allele marks likely C*06:02 carriage. About two-thirds of C*06:02 carriers never develop psoriasis.

interpretations.CC: No copies of the HLA-C*06:02 tag allele. Average odds of psoriasis at this locus are at the population baseline. Psoriasis still occurs in non-carriers — dozens of other loci and environmental triggers contribute — and a tag SNP is an imperfect proxy for direct HLA typing.
interpretations.CT: One copy of the T allele tagging HLA-C*06:02. Linked on average to higher odds of psoriasis than non-carriers: a moderate to large shift, with a stronger association for early-onset and guttate forms. Most carriers never develop psoriasis; this is a susceptibility marker, not a determination.
interpretations.TT: Two copies of the T allele tagging HLA-C*06:02. Homozygous carriage is associated with higher average odds of psoriasis than a single copy, again weighted toward early-onset disease. The association is probabilistic: many people with this genotype remain unaffected throughout life.

citations.label: Nair et al., Am J Hum Genet 2006

title: Systemic lupus erythematosus · STAT4
summary: STAT4 helps immune cells respond to interferon and IL-12 signals. rs7574865 T is one of the most repeated non-HLA risk links for systemic lupus. Each copy is linked to higher odds: a small to moderate shift. It has a smaller link to rheumatoid arthritis. On GRCh38, T is the risk-linked reference base, while G is common.

interpretations.GG: Two copies of the common G allele. Average odds of lupus at this variant are the population baseline. Lupus susceptibility involves many genetic variants plus hormonal and environmental factors, so this single result says little on its own.
interpretations.GT: One copy of the risk-associated T allele, carried by roughly a quarter to a third of many populations. Associated on average with higher odds of systemic lupus erythematosus: a small to moderate shift. The increase for rheumatoid arthritis is smaller. Lupus is rare, so absolute risk remains low; this is one small factor among many.
interpretations.TT: Two copies of the risk-associated T allele. Associated on average with higher odds of systemic lupus erythematosus compared with GG: a moderate shift. Because lupus affects well under 1% of most populations, absolute risk stays low even for this genotype; this is one small factor among many influences.

citations.label: Remmers et al., N Engl J Med 2007

title: Ankylosing spondylitis · HLA-B27 tag
summary: HLA-B27 has one of the strongest HLA links to disease. Carriers have far higher average odds of ankylosing spondylitis than non-carriers, yet most never develop it. rs4349859 A tags likely HLA-B*27:05. It is an imperfect stand-in, mainly outside populations with European ancestry. Direct HLA-B27 typing from blood gives the clearest result.

interpretations.GG: No copies of the HLA-B27 tag, so B27 is likely absent. Ankylosing spondylitis can occur without B27, but its average rate is much lower. Tag variants do not track every HLA-B*27 type well. Direct HLA typing gives a clearer answer.
interpretations.AG: One A copy, which tags HLA-B*27:05. B27 has a strong link to ankylosing spondylitis and is found in most cases, yet most carriers never develop the condition. The tag is less reliable in some ancestry groups. Direct HLA-B27 typing gives a clearer answer.
interpretations.AA: Two copies of the A allele tagging HLA-B*27:05, a rare genotype consistent with B27 on both chromosomes. The association with ankylosing spondylitis is strong on a relative scale, but most B27 carriers, including homozygotes, never develop the condition. Direct HLA typing remains the definitive measure of B27 status.

title: Thyroid disease from the immune system · CTLA4 (CT60)
summary: CTLA-4 is a brake on T-cell activation, and the CT60 variant (rs3087243) in its 3’ region is a replicated susceptibility factor for autoimmune thyroid disease. The common G allele is the susceptibility allele. Each copy is associated with higher odds of Graves’ disease, a small shift, and with weaker associations with autoimmune hypothyroidism and type 1 diabetes. The A allele is associated with lower average odds.

interpretations.AA: Two copies of A, linked to the lowest average odds of Graves' disease and autoimmune thyroid disease at this locus. The effect is small. Many other genes and environmental factors shape thyroid autoimmunity, so this result changes chance only slightly.
interpretations.AG: One copy of each allele, linked to average odds between AA and GG. Each G copy is linked to higher odds of Graves’ disease: a small shift. It is one factor among many causes of thyroid autoimmunity.
interpretations.GG: Two copies of the susceptibility-associated G allele, the most common genotype in many populations. Associated on average with higher odds of Graves’ disease than AA: a moderate shift, with weaker increases for autoimmune hypothyroidism. This remains a modest probabilistic shift, not a prediction.

title: Inflammatory bowel disease · IL23R R381Q
summary: IL23R makes a receptor for interleukin-23, an immune signal involved in gut swelling and damage. The rs11209026 A allele (R381Q) weakens this signal and is protective. Carriers have lower average odds of Crohn’s disease: a moderate to large shift. Studies also link it to lower odds of ulcerative colitis and psoriasis. This finding helped guide research on the IL-23 pathway.

interpretations.GG: Two copies of the common G allele (381R), found in the large majority of people. Average odds of Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis at this variant are the population baseline. Overall IBD susceptibility involves more than a hundred other loci plus environmental factors.
interpretations.AG: One copy of the protective A allele (381Q), carried by roughly 5-7% of people of European ancestry. Associated on average with lower odds of Crohn’s disease: a moderate to large shift. It is also linked to lower odds of ulcerative colitis and psoriasis. Protection is partial — carriers can still develop IBD.
interpretations.AA: Two copies of protective A (381Q), a rare result. It is linked to much lower average odds of Crohn's disease and related inflammatory conditions at this locus. It lowers chance but does not rule out inflammatory bowel disease.
